title: Static vs Dynamic Typing
summary: When type checks happen — compile-time vs runtime — and what that trades off. The most foundational type-system distinction, and the one every other Topic in this group builds on.

slides.markdown:
Every value in every program has a type — the question this Topic answers is **when does anything check it?** Static typing checks types before the program ever runs, at compile time. Dynamic typing checks types as the program executes, at the moment an operation actually happens.

`"5" + 3` in Java fails to compile — the type checker rejects it before any code runs. The same expression in Python runs fine syntactically but raises `TypeError` the instant that line executes, because Python only discovers the type mismatch when it's actually adding a string to an int.

This single distinction — checked ahead of time vs checked in the moment — shapes tooling, refactoring safety, and how early a bug surfaces, and it's the axis every other Topic in this group assumes you already understand.

**Static typing** verifies that every operation is applied to a value of the expected type *before* the program runs — the type checker walks the whole program's source and either accepts it or rejects it with a compile error. If it accepts, every typed operation in the program is guaranteed type-correct before a single line executes.

**Dynamic typing** carries type information on the *value* at runtime and checks it lazily, the moment an operation is attempted. There's no separate pass that verifies the whole program up front — a type error only surfaces when the offending line actually executes, which might be five minutes into a running program, on a code path that hasn't been exercised yet.

The distinction is entirely about *when*, not about whether types exist — every language has types; static and dynamic differ only in the moment those types get checked against how they're used.

slides.sectionTitle: Compile-time gate vs runtime tag check
slides.markdown:
Take the exact same buggy call — passing a string where a number is expected — through both models.

In a statically typed language, the compiler has a type signature for the function (`add(x: number, y: number): number`) and checks the call site's argument types against it *before generating any executable code*. A mismatched call never becomes a running program at all — the gate stops it upstream of execution.

In a dynamically typed language, there is no such gate. The program compiles or is directly interpreted with no type check at that call site. Only when the function body actually tries to use the bad argument — say, `x + y` where `x` turns out to be a string — does the runtime inspect the value's tag, discover the mismatch, and raise an error, *at that exact moment in execution*, potentially deep inside a production run.

![A type error rejected at a compile-time gate before execution, versus the same error only caught by a runtime type-tag check](assets/compile-time-vs-runtime-gate.svg)

slides.sectionTitle: The same bug, caught two ways

slides.markdown:
Three concrete payoffs, not just "fewer bugs" in the abstract:

- **Earlier error detection.** A type mismatch on a rarely-exercised code path is caught at build time for everyone, instead of waiting for that path to run in production for the first time — which for a rare branch can be months after deployment.
- **IDE tooling.** Autocomplete, "find all usages," and inline error squiggles are only possible because the IDE can statically know a value's type without running any code — a dynamically typed value's type is often genuinely unknowable until runtime, so tooling can only guess.
- **Refactor safety.** Rename a field or change a function's parameter type, and the compiler immediately lists every call site that's now wrong. In a dynamically typed codebase, the equivalent refactor relies on test coverage (or a text search) to find every affected spot, and a missed call site fails silently until that path runs.

All three reduce to the same underlying fact: a static type checker has already examined every code path once, even the ones your tests haven't.

The trade isn't one-sided. Dynamic typing removes the type checker as a gate, and that removal has real value:

- **Flexibility.** A function can genuinely accept "anything with a `.read()` method" or return different shapes depending on runtime conditions, without contorting a type signature to express it — some patterns (duck typing, heavily data-driven code) are naturally awkward to state as a fixed static type.
- **Less ceremony.** No type annotations to write and keep in sync with the code as it evolves; a function's signature is just its parameter names, and changing behavior doesn't require also updating a type declaration in lockstep.
- **Faster prototyping.** Sketching an idea in Python or Ruby means you can run code before every type is nailed down — useful when you're still exploring what the shapes of your data even are, and premature type commitments would just get rewritten anyway.

The honest framing: dynamic typing defers a cost (catching type errors) in exchange for removing a cost (declaring and maintaining types) — which one wins depends on whether the code will live long enough, and be touched by enough people, for the deferred cost to come due.

**Gradual typing** lets you opt into static checks incrementally on top of a dynamically typed language, rather than forcing an all-or-nothing choice. TypeScript compiles to JavaScript and lets you annotate as much or as little as you want — an unannotated variable defaults to `any`, which opts that specific value back out of static checking entirely. Python's type hints (`def add(x: int, y: int) -> int`) are pure annotations that the interpreter ignores at runtime; a separate tool (mypy, Pyright) reads them and does the static checking as a distinct step. Sorbet does the same for Ruby.

The honest limitation: gradual typing's guarantees are only as strong as your annotation coverage. An `any`-typed value in TypeScript, or an untyped function in a mostly-typed Python codebase, is a hole in the static net — code can flow through it with zero checking, and a bug there behaves exactly like it would in a fully dynamic language.

Gradual typing is genuinely useful specifically because it lets a large existing dynamic codebase migrate toward static guarantees incrementally, module by module, instead of requiring a rewrite.

"Static typing" gets oversold as "no runtime errors," and that's false. A static type checker verifies that types *line up according to its rules* — it says nothing about values that are legally typed but semantically wrong.

Two classic examples that compile perfectly in a statically typed language and still crash at runtime: **null dereferences** — a `String` field that's legally `null` in Java compiles fine everywhere, and a `NullPointerException` at runtime is still a type-correct program (until Kotlin/Swift-style null safety, covered in a later Topic, makes nullability part of the type itself). **Bad casts** — `(String) someObject` compiles if `someObject`'s *declared* type could plausibly be cast, but throws `ClassCastException` at runtime if the actual object isn't really a `String`.

The accurate claim: static typing catches type-mismatch bugs *the checker's type system is expressive enough to describe* — before runtime. It doesn't catch logic bugs, null-related bugs (unless the type system is null-aware), or unsafe casts. Overselling this is a real interview tell — a candidate who says "static typing means no runtime errors" hasn't actually used a null-permissive statically typed language in production.

slides.sectionTitle: Statically vs dynamically typed language families
slides.markdown:
| | Statically typed (Java, Rust) | Dynamically typed (Python, Ruby, JS) |
|---|---|---|
| **Type errors surface** | At compile time, before running | At runtime, when the operation executes |
| **Type annotations** | Usually required (or inferred, Topic 3) | Optional/absent, unless using gradual typing |
| **Refactor confidence** | Compiler flags every broken call site | Relies on tests/search to find broken call sites |
| **Iteration speed early on** | Slower — must satisfy the checker to run at all | Faster — run first, discover mismatches as you go |

This table is a generalization, not a law — Rust's static checker famously also enforces memory-safety rules beyond typing, and Python's ecosystem increasingly leans on gradual typing (mypy) to claw back some of the static column's benefits without abandoning the language.

slides.sectionTitle: What bugs would a type checker have caught here?
slides.markdown:
This exact prompt — a broken snippet, "what would a type checker catch" — is common enough to prepare a method for. The strong move: identify every place a value's *assumed* type doesn't match what the code actually does with it, then classify each as "a static checker would catch this" or "a static checker wouldn't, because it's a value-level bug, not a type-level one."

Example: given `def total(items): return sum(item.price for item in items)` called with a list containing one plain dict instead of an object with a `.price` attribute — a static checker with a expressive-enough type system (requiring all elements to satisfy an interface with `.price`) would catch this at the call site, because the dict doesn't satisfy that interface. But if every item genuinely has a `.price` attribute and one of them is `None` because upstream code failed to set it, that's a null-safety bug, not a plain type mismatch — a checker only catches it if its type system tracks nullability explicitly (Topic 7 in this group).

Naming that second distinction — "this needs null-aware types, not just typing" — is exactly the kind of precision that reads as senior in this line of questioning.

slides.sectionTitle: Why this Topic anchors the group
slides.markdown:
Every remaining Topic in this group assumes you can place a language on the static/dynamic axis first, because several of them only make sense on one side of it. Type inference (next Topic) is a static-typing feature — a dynamically typed language has nothing to infer, since it never checks types ahead of time at all. Generics and variance are compile-time constructs, meaningful specifically because a static checker needs to verify them before running. Structural vs nominal typing applies to both, but plays out very differently — a dynamic language's "structural typing" is really just duck typing with zero checking at all, discovered only at the moment of use.

So before any of those Topics, the useful checkpoint is: for a given language, can you say precisely when its type checks happen, and does that language make any static guarantee at all before running? Get that right, and the rest of the group's vocabulary attaches to something concrete instead of floating free.
